lecture.title: Introduction to Syntax
lecture.scope: Lecture 6. Original practice sentences apply the taught patterns, structures, and theoretical distinctions. Incorrect labels and misleading examples are corrected rather than reproduced as answer keys.
lecture.exam_alignment: Concept-based practice. No past paper or official examination blueprint was supplied.
lecture.answer_model: Single best answer. answer_id refers to an option id, not its displayed position. Preserve option ids when shuffling.
lecture.display_guidance: In learning mode, display explanation followed by example after the learner answers. Source slides and clarification notes can appear in a reference panel.
lecture.terminology: SVA exercises state the slide’s convention of displaying an expressed adverbial, without implying it must be obligatory. Structural sentence exercises use traditional finite-clause counts with unambiguous examples. Classical TG terminology is presented within its historical theoretical context.

references.title: Subject complements
references.supports: Subject complements characterize or identify the subject; they are not consonants or automatically direct objects.

references.title: Fronting
references.supports: Fronting and subject–verb inversion are distinct; a fronted prepositional phrase need not reverse subject and verb.

references.title: Inversion
references.supports: Inversion concerns a change from ordinary grammatical ordering, commonly subject–verb order.

references.title: Sentence Punctuation Patterns
references.supports: The semicolon-plus-however pattern joins independent clauses; however is not one of the seven coordinators.

references.author: Noam Chomsky
references.title: Syntactic Structures
references.supports: The 1957 publication milestone is distinguished from subsequent classical generative developments.

references.author: Noam Chomsky
references.title: Aspects of the Theory of Syntax
references.supports: Later classical generative theory is not treated as an unchanged complete 1957 framework. Technical descriptions in the questions are paraphrases of the supplied lecture, not claimed quotations from the book.

clarifications.note: C means complement, not consonant. To school is not the direct object of goes. A means adverbial rather than only a word-class adverb. Optional slowly does not prove an obligatory SVA frame; the four patterns are not exhaustive.

Constituents are structural units rather than arbitrary adjacent strings. Immediate constituents are relative to a level. Words are terminal units only in the lecture’s selected word-based analysis, not the smallest units of all grammar.

Loose/periodic labels describe rhetorical arrangement. Parallelism is tested as matching comparable forms; a shared infinitival to is permitted, and no universal ban on every mixed-category coordination is inferred.

Oranges grow in California has no direct object. In California is a locative PP, not a moved object. Fronting it while retaining oranges grow is not subject–verb inversion. Full-verb inversion examples are identified as marked constructions.

Typical communicative purposes and grammatical sentence forms are distinguished. The king is dead! is declarative in structure despite an exclamatory use; a polite request can have interrogative form.

Clause counts determine structural labels, not length or the presence of and. A compound subject or coordinated predicate can occur in a traditional simple sentence. This exercise set avoids disputes over non-finite clause counts.
However is not a coordinating conjunction. The illustrated compound pattern uses independent clause; however, independent clause.

The 1957 Syntactic Structures milestone is distinguished from later classical deep/surface terminology. These levels are theoretical syntactic representations, not mental motives, identical meanings, anatomical boxes, or acoustic recordings. Transformations are not unrestricted word shuffling.
Active/passive pairs can retain central event relationships while differing in focus or explicit agent information. An omitted agent is not assumed to preserve every detail.

questions.question: What is the central concern of syntax in this lecture?
questions.explanation: Syntax investigates structural combinations and grammatical relationships. It goes beyond knowing individual words to explaining how they form larger units.
questions.example: The arrangement of she, has, and arrived matters in “She has arrived.”

options.text: How words are alphabetized in dictionaries
How words and phrases are organized into sentence structures
How written letters developed historically
How individual speech sounds travel through air

questions.question: Which sense of arrangement is relevant to syntax?
questions.explanation: Syntactic arrangement concerns relationships among words and phrases. It is not merely a visual or alphabetical ordering.
questions.example: The student read the book contains a subject, verb, and object in a particular arrangement.

options.text: The order in which books are placed on a shelf
The visual choice of a text’s font
The grammatical organization of linguistic elements
The alphabetical sorting of a word list

questions.question: A researcher compares “The boy jumped happily” with “Happily, the boy jumped.” Which aspect of syntax is illustrated most directly?
questions.explanation: The modifier occupies different positions while the basic event remains recognizable. The examples show that more than one arrangement can be acceptable.
questions.example: The boy happily jumped gives another placement in the slide.

options.text: The replacement of one consonant phoneme
Variation in the placement of a modifying expression
The addition of a plural suffix
The creation of a new dictionary meaning for boy

questions.question: What do the three placements of “happily” on slide 3 show about English syntax?
questions.explanation: Syntactic flexibility is constrained rather than unlimited. Acceptable positions depend on the construction, and placement can also affect focus or interpretation.
questions.example: A modifier may occur before or after a clause without licensing arbitrary movement of all its words.

options.text: All sentence rearrangements must change every grammatical relation.
Some expressions allow more than one grammatical position.
A sentence has no structure if it contains an adverb.
Every English word can move to any position freely.

questions.question: Which question is primarily syntactic?
questions.explanation: The correct question concerns sentence organization. The alternatives focus on physical properties or production of speech sounds.
questions.example: Identifying the subject in “The small bird sang” requires structural analysis.

options.text: Which words form the subject phrase in this sentence?
How many milliseconds does the vowel last?
Which frequency band is strongest in the recording?
Where does the tongue touch during this consonant?

questions.question: Why is a list of word meanings insufficient for explaining a sentence’s structure?
questions.explanation: Knowing the vocabulary does not specify how the words combine. Syntax explains such relationships as subject, predicate, and object.
questions.example: Dog, chased, and cat permit different relationships in “The dog chased the cat” and its reversal.

options.text: The words also enter ordered and hierarchical grammatical relationships.
Dictionary order determines each word’s subject or object role.
Syntax can be studied only when all words have identical meanings.
Every word loses its meaning in a sentence.

questions.question: What ability is highlighted by the lecture’s discussion of an unlimited set of possible sentences?
questions.explanation: A generative capacity concerns the range of possible expressions. Each actual sentence remains finite and is interpreted through shared linguistic knowledge.
questions.example: A listener can understand a new sentence about a robot borrowing a bicycle.

options.text: Making an individual sentence infinitely long in actual speech
Using words without any constraints on arrangement
Producing and understanding novel sentences through a linguistic system
Memorizing every complete sentence before using language

questions.question: Why does an unlimited range of possible sentences not require an unlimited number of memorized sentence entries?
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes productive knowledge rather than a fixed list of messages. Familiar elements can be combined into structures not encountered before.
questions.example: A speaker can add another descriptive phrase to an existing sentence pattern.

options.text: Rules and reusable elements can support new combinations.
All speakers must already have heard every possible combination.
A dictionary includes every possible complete sentence.
Every new sentence must be an unanalyzable sound.

questions.question: How should the lecture’s description of the sentence as the highest grammatical unit be understood?
questions.explanation: Sentence grammar can take the sentence as its largest main unit while other approaches study connected texts and interaction. The teaching scale is not a denial of discourse.
questions.example: A paragraph contains relationships that extend beyond one sentence.

options.text: It means every sentence must contain several paragraphs.
It proves that paragraphs and conversations have no organization.
It identifies a focus of sentence grammar without denying larger discourse organization.
It makes word formation unrelated to grammar.

questions.question: Which description best captures what a syntactic account should explain?
questions.explanation: A useful analysis explains how parts combine and which patterns the language licenses. Printed length and truth are separate questions.
questions.example: An account of questions should explain possible auxiliary positions, not just count their words.

options.text: Permitted structures and grammatical relationships, including both constraints and variation
Only the number of printed spaces in each sentence
Only whether a statement is factually true
Only a speaker’s preference for formal vocabulary

questions.question: What is structural ambiguity?
questions.explanation: The same word sequence can permit different structures. The ambiguity is then linked to how the parts group or attach, rather than merely to a word with several senses.
questions.example: I saw the man with a telescope can permit two attachment readings.

options.text: A spelling error that removes every possible interpretation
A difference in loudness between two recordings
More than one interpretation arising from alternative grammatical groupings
A word list arranged in two fonts

questions.question: In “I saw the man with a telescope,” which reading attaches “with a telescope” to the seeing event?
questions.explanation: The phrase identifies an instrument for seeing in this reading. Another grouping can connect it with the man instead.
questions.example: I used binoculars to see the bird makes the instrument interpretation explicit.

options.text: The man was standing beside a telescope owner.
The man had a telescope with him.
The word man means a telescope.
I used a telescope to see the man.

questions.question: Which version most clearly expresses the reading that the man possessed or carried the telescope?
questions.explanation: The relative clause explicitly connects the telescope with the man. The alternatives connect a telescope with the observer’s seeing.
questions.example: I noticed the child who held the umbrella similarly makes the possession relation clear.

options.text: I looked through a telescope and saw the man.
I used my telescope to observe the man.
I saw the man who was carrying a telescope.
Using a telescope, I saw the man.

questions.question: What makes the two telescope readings structural rather than simply different definitions of telescope?
questions.explanation: The instrument itself can have the same basic meaning in both readings. The difference concerns which element the phrase modifies or completes.
questions.example: A phrase can describe a participant in one structure and an action in another.

options.text: The phrase attaches to different parts of the sentence.
Telescope must change from noun to conjunction.
The sentence must have a different number of sound segments.
The two readings require different spellings of the same word.

questions.question: What are paraphrases in the lecture’s introductory discussion?
questions.explanation: Paraphrase concerns a relationship in meaning despite differences of wording or structure. Context and detail still matter.
questions.example: The teacher praised Ali and Ali was praised by the teacher describe the same basic event.

options.text: Sequences with the same number of words regardless of meaning
Different expressions that convey closely corresponding content in a relevant interpretation
Two sentences that must always have opposite truth values
Expressions with identical spelling but unrelated meanings

questions.question: Which sentence best preserves the participants and tense of “The teacher praised Ali” while changing it to passive voice?
questions.explanation: The passive preserves who praised whom and the past-time interpretation. The alternatives reverse roles or change tense.
questions.example: Sara opened the gate corresponds to The gate was opened by Sara.

options.text: Ali will be praised by the teacher.
Ali praised the teacher.
Ali was praised by the teacher.
The teacher was praised by Ali.

questions.question: Why are active and passive versions not necessarily identical in every communicative effect?
questions.explanation: Related content does not require identical information structure. A passive may emphasize the affected participant, and an omitted agent can reduce explicit information.
questions.example: The window was broken does not name the breaker.

options.text: They can foreground different participants or omit information about the agent.
A change of voice necessarily changes past tense into future tense.
Passive voice always reverses who performs the action.
An active clause can never describe the same event as a passive clause.

questions.question: Which pair gives examples of grammatical relations mentioned in the lecture’s discussion?
questions.explanation: Grammatical relations concern how constituents function in a structure. They are not the same as physical sound measures or word-internal positions.
questions.example: In “Sara read a book,” Sara is subject and a book is object.

options.text: Prefix and suffix
Pitch and intensity
Font size and page number
Subject and object

questions.question: What is the grammatical subject in “The child was helped by the teacher”?
questions.explanation: The child occupies the subject position in the passive clause. The participant performing the helping appears in the by-phrase.
questions.example: The book is subject in “The book was read by Ali.”

options.text: The child
helped by
by the teacher
the teacher

questions.question: Why is subject not simply defined as the person who performs the action?
questions.explanation: Subject is a grammatical relation, while agent concerns a participant’s role in an event. They often align in active clauses but need not align in passives.
questions.example: In “Ali was praised,” Ali is subject but does not perform the praising.

options.text: Only clauses without verbs can have subjects.
Every subject must be an adjective.
The agent is always the last word in a sentence.
A passive subject may represent the affected participant rather than the agent.

questions.question: What changes when “The dog chased the cat” becomes “The cat chased the dog”?
questions.explanation: The words remain familiar, but their arrangement changes who is subject and who is object. The described chasing event is correspondingly different.
questions.example: Ali thanked Sara and Sara thanked Ali assign the participants different roles.

options.text: The sentences become phonetic rather than syntactic structures.
The grammatical relations of the two noun phrases change.
The two nouns necessarily acquire new dictionary definitions.
The verb must change its tense solely because the nouns change positions.

questions.question: Which task best combines the three kinds of syntactic knowledge named on slide 4?
questions.explanation: The slide lists structural ambiguity, paraphrase relations, and grammatical functions. The correct task directly investigates all three concerns.
questions.example: A comparison can ask how a phrase attaches and how subject and object roles are preserved in a paraphrase.

options.text: Measure vowel length, pitch, and intensity in one recording.
Explain an ambiguous grouping, compare a paraphrase, and identify grammatical relations.
Count letters, sort headwords, and choose dictionary page sizes.
Name a speaker’s age, occupation, and place of birth.

questions.question: What do S and V represent in the elementary pattern SV?
questions.explanation: The labels identify major clause elements. They are grammatical functions, not speech-sound categories.
questions.example: Birds sing contains a subject and a verb.

options.text: Sound and voicing
Subject and verb
Sentence and vowel
Suffix and vocabulary

questions.question: Which sentence most clearly illustrates the basic SV pattern with no object or added adverbial?
questions.explanation: The baby supplies the subject and slept the verb. The other options contain an object, a subject complement, or an extra adverbial.
questions.example: The students laughed is another uncomplicated SV example.

options.text: The baby was cheerful.
The baby held a toy.
The baby slept.
The baby slept peacefully.

questions.question: What does O represent in SVO?
questions.explanation: The object is a grammatical constituent related to the verb. The label does not refer simply to any word following a verb.
questions.example: A book is the object in “She read a book.”

options.text: Order
Orthography
Optional vowel
Object

questions.question: Which sentence most clearly illustrates SVO?
questions.explanation: Sara is subject, opened is verb, and the door is direct object. The other sentences do not have that same three-part relation.
questions.example: Ali kicked the ball also illustrates SVO.

options.text: Sara opened the door.
Sara went to school.
Sara became tired.
Sara arrived.

questions.question: What is the direct object in “The student read the article”?
questions.explanation: The article is the noun phrase selected as the object of read. The student is the subject performing the reading in this active clause.
questions.example: In “She bought a notebook,” a notebook is the direct object.

options.text: The student
the article
read
the student read

questions.question: Why is “She goes to school” a misleading SVO example?
questions.explanation: The noun school is within the prepositional phrase headed by to. It is not the same relation as the door after opened.
questions.example: She visits the school has a direct object; she goes to school contains a directional phrase.

options.text: Every expression following a verb is automatically its direct object.
Goes has no grammatical relationship with the rest of the clause.
School is a finite verb in this sentence.
To school is a prepositional phrase expressing direction, not a direct object of goes.

questions.question: What should C stand for in the lecture’s pattern SVC?
questions.explanation: The slide’s consonant label is an error. C identifies a clause complement, such as an expression characterizing the subject after a linking verb.
questions.example: Nice is a subject complement in “She looks nice.”

options.text: Conjunction
Complement
Capital letter
Consonant

questions.question: Which sentence most clearly illustrates SVC?
questions.explanation: Tired characterizes the students after the linking verb seem. It does not name a separate participant receiving an action.
questions.example: The room became quiet is another SVC example.

options.text: The students laughed.
The students seem tired.
The students carried chairs.
The students arrived yesterday.

questions.question: In “Sara is a teacher,” what is the function of “a teacher”?
questions.explanation: The expression identifies Sara after the linking verb is. It is not an object affected by an action.
questions.example: A doctor has a similar function in “Ali became a doctor.”

options.text: Direct object
Directional adverbial
Subject complement
Subject

questions.question: Which distinction separates an object from the subject complement in “Sara is a teacher”?
questions.explanation: Position alone is insufficient. The relation to the verb and subject helps determine the grammatical function.
questions.example: The teacher in “Sara met the teacher” is an object, unlike a teacher after is.

options.text: An object must always be an inanimate thing.
Any phrase after is is a direct object by position alone.
A complement must always be one adjective.
The complement describes or identifies the subject rather than functioning as a separate object.

questions.question: What is the most accurate expansion of A in the lecture’s elementary SVA notation?
questions.explanation: Adverbial is a function, while adverb is a word class. A location, direction, time, or manner expression may have different structural forms.
questions.example: Here and in Lahore can each function as locative expressions.

options.text: Adverbial, which can be realized by a word or a phrase
Article only
Agent only
Adjective only

questions.question: Using the lecture’s convention of showing an expressed adverbial as A, which analysis fits “You eat slowly”?
questions.explanation: Slowly gives manner information about the eating. The pattern records the expressed adverbial rather than treating it as a direct object.
questions.example: She spoke clearly also includes a manner adverbial.

options.text: You is S, eat is V, and slowly is A.
You is S, eat is O, and slowly is V.
You is A, eat is S, and slowly is C.
You is O, eat is C, and slowly is S.

questions.question: What qualification is needed when using “You eat slowly” as SVA?
questions.explanation: The slide’s simplified pattern records the elements present. It should not imply that every adverbial in an SVA-labelled example is obligatory.
questions.example: You eat is grammatical without the added manner expression.

options.text: Slowly is optional, so another analysis can describe an SV core with an added adverbial.
The sentence becomes ungrammatical whenever slowly is omitted.
Slowly must be a noun because it occurs last.
Eat requires a manner adverbial in every sentence.

questions.question: Which expression functions as the directional adverbial in “She went to school”?
questions.explanation: The whole prepositional phrase expresses the destination. School is contained inside it, so the phrase must be analysed as a unit.
questions.example: To the station can likewise express a destination after went.

options.text: went
school as an independent direct object
She
to school

questions.question: Which pair contrasts a direct object with an adverbial most clearly?
questions.explanation: The first pair directly contrasts a noun phrase functioning as object with a directional prepositional phrase. The other pairs compare like functions.
questions.example: The park after visited differs structurally from to the park after went.

options.text: the school in “She visited the school” and to school in “She went to school”
tired in “She seems tired” and happy in “She seems happy”
slept in “He slept” and laughed in “He laughed”
Sara in “Sara smiled” and Ali in “Ali laughed”

questions.question: Why should the four patterns on slide 6 not be treated as an exhaustive inventory of English clause structures?
questions.explanation: A short teaching list provides a starting point. It does not establish that all other grammatical patterns are impossible.
questions.example: Longer expressions and additional complement patterns require a fuller description.

options.text: English clauses cannot contain more than one phrase.
Any pattern not on the slide must be ungrammatical.
Every English sentence must contain exactly three words.
They are selected introductory patterns rather than every possible structure.

questions.question: In “The flowers are beautiful,” which analysis is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Beautiful describes the subject after the linking verb. A subject complement can be adjectival rather than noun-headed.
questions.example: The sky is clear has the same broad SVC pattern.

options.text: “The flowers” is the subject, “are” is the linking verb, and “beautiful” is the subject complement.
Beautiful is a direct object affected by are.
The flowers is object, are is subject, and beautiful is verb.
The sentence has no complement because beautiful is an adjective.

questions.question: Which procedure best supports accurate identification of S, V, O, C, and A?
questions.explanation: Functions depend on relationships, not just positions or word count. A multiword phrase can realize one clause element.
questions.example: The little boy is one subject phrase, while very tired can be one complement.

options.text: Classify a phrase solely by its number of syllables.
Assume each word represents a different clause function.
Examine the verb’s construction and the relationships among whole constituents.
Label every final word O regardless of its structure.

questions.question: What is a constituent in the lecture’s introductory account?
questions.explanation: Constituents can be words or larger groups. Their status depends on how the structure is organized, not simply on their visual proximity.
questions.example: The little boy can function as one subject constituent.

options.text: Any arbitrary run of neighboring letters
A unit functioning as part of a larger grammatical structure
Only a whole paragraph containing several sentences
Only a morpheme that cannot stand alone

questions.question: What does hierarchical sentence structure mean?
questions.explanation: The lecture describes sentences divided into phrases and phrases into further units. This gives structure beyond a flat word sequence.
questions.example: The noun phrase the old house contains a head noun and modifiers.

options.text: All words have equal relationships to every other word.
The first printed word must contain every later word.
Larger units contain smaller units organized within them.
A sentence is only an alphabetically ordered list.

questions.question: In “The little boy opened the door,” which expression is a clear subject constituent?
questions.explanation: The noun phrase functions together as subject. The alternatives cross major structural boundaries without matching that requested function.
questions.example: The small bird is similarly a subject constituent in “The small bird sang.”

options.text: boy opened
little boy opened the
opened the
The little boy

questions.question: In a traditional initial division into subject and predicate, what are the immediate constituents of “The child laughed”?
questions.explanation: Immediate constituents are the units directly below the structure being divided. At this level, the subject phrase and predicate form the two parts.
questions.example: The bird and sang are an analogous first division of “The bird sang.”

options.text: “The child” and “laughed”
The child laughed and an unspoken object
“Child” and “the”
“The” and “child”

questions.question: What makes constituent analysis more than a word count?
questions.explanation: Counting words gives the size of a string, not its full organization. Constituent analysis investigates internal groupings.
questions.example: The three words in the old house form one noun phrase, not three unrelated clause elements.

options.text: It replaces grammar with spelling length.
It requires every word to belong to a separate sentence.
It identifies which words group together and how the groups relate.
It treats all adjacent sequences as equivalent units.

questions.question: In “the book on the desk,” which expression is embedded inside the larger noun phrase?
questions.explanation: The prepositional phrase modifies book within the larger unit. It illustrates one phrase contained inside another.
questions.example: The student from Lahore contains the embedded phrase from Lahore.

options.text: desk the
on the desk
the book on the
book on

questions.question: Why are immediate constituents relative to a chosen level of analysis?
questions.explanation: Immediate describes a local relationship in a hierarchy. The units directly contained in a clause are not necessarily the same units obtained by dividing its noun phrase.
questions.example: The child is a subject constituent, and the and child can be examined within that phrase.

options.text: The same unit must always be the largest structure in every sentence.
Only single letters can be immediate constituents.
A phrase cannot have any internal constituents.
A unit can be a direct part of one structure while itself containing smaller parts.

questions.question: How many written words occur in the slide’s example “My friend came home late last night”?
questions.explanation: The words are My, friend, came, home, late, last, and night. The count follows the lecture’s word-based example.
questions.example: My friend supplies two words within the seven-word sequence.

options.text: Five
Eight
Seven
Six

questions.question: Which expression functions as subject in “My friend came home late last night”?
questions.explanation: My friend is the noun phrase occupying the subject role. The other expressions belong to the predicate or temporal information.
questions.example: My sister is subject in “My sister arrived yesterday.”

options.text: came home
home late
last night
My friend

questions.question: In the slide’s word-based analysis, what are called ultimate constituents?
questions.explanation: Ultimate is used for the units where this particular division stops. The description must specify the chosen analytical level.
questions.example: My and friend are separate words in the slide’s terminal word sequence.

options.text: The entire sentence treated as one word
Only the punctuation marks at sentence boundaries
The individual words reached at the endpoint of that analysis
Only the two largest clause parts

questions.question: Why should the slide’s words-as-ultimate-constituents example not imply that words are the smallest grammatical units in every analysis?
questions.explanation: A word-level syntactic endpoint is not a universal claim about all grammar. Lecture 4 already distinguishes morphemes within words.
questions.example: Boys is one word but can contain boy plus plural -s.

options.text: Only phonetic analysis can recognize the existence of words.
Morphological analysis can identify smaller meaningful units within words.
Every word is necessarily one indivisible morpheme.
Sentences cannot be divided into phrases.

questions.question: Which pair best illustrates a larger constituent and a phrase nested within it?
questions.explanation: The larger noun phrase includes the smaller prepositional phrase. Their categories and boundaries can be stated separately.
questions.example: The house near the school contains near the school.

options.text: the student from and Lahore the
“the student from Lahore” and “from Lahore”
student from and from
student and the student as one morpheme

questions.question: Why should arbitrary adjacent strings not automatically be called constituents in a given analysis?
questions.explanation: Adjacency is common but not sufficient. A proposed grouping needs to fit the organization of the sentence.
questions.example: The little boy is a plausible subject unit, while boy opened crosses the subject–predicate boundary.

options.text: A string can be a unit only if it contains one syllable.
Constituent status requires evidence that the string forms a structural unit.
Every pair of adjacent words always has the same grammatical role.
Only printed brackets can create a grammatical grouping.

questions.question: A student analyses a sentence only as a left-to-right list of words. What key aspect from slide 7 is missing?
questions.explanation: A list captures sequence but not hierarchy. The lecture explicitly includes division into phrases and further embedded phrases.
questions.example: A sequence containing a noun phrase and its modifier requires more structure than a list alone shows.

options.text: The dictionary order of its nouns
The fact that words can be written with capital letters
The grouping of phrases within larger phrases and clauses
The number of letters printed in the sentence

questions.question: What characterizes a loose sentence in the lecture’s rhetorical classification?
questions.explanation: Loose concerns how information unfolds, not an absence of grammar. The main point appears before additional detail.
questions.example: We reached Lahore that morning after a long journey places the arrival first.

options.text: It must contain several spelling mistakes.
The main clause is deliberately withheld until the end.
It must have exactly one subject word and no modifiers.
The main clause is presented early, followed by added material.

questions.question: What characterizes a periodic sentence in the lecture’s rhetorical classification?
questions.explanation: The arrangement delays the central statement and can create anticipation. It is a rhetorical description, not a count of clauses.
questions.example: After a long journey through the rain, we reached Lahore delays the main clause.

options.text: The sentence must repeat the same word at equal intervals.
Every clause must end with a semicolon.
The main clause is delayed until after introductory material.
The main clause must always be the first expression.

questions.question: Which sentence most clearly places the main point first in a loose arrangement?
questions.explanation: The arrival statement is available before the added journey detail. The other examples lead with material before the main clause.
questions.example: She completed the task before explaining its difficulties similarly gives the central action early.

options.text: We reached Lahore that morning, after a tiring overnight journey.
Although the journey was tiring, we reached Lahore that morning.
After a tiring overnight journey, we reached Lahore that morning.
When the overnight journey ended, we reached Lahore.

questions.question: Which sentence most clearly delays the main clause in a periodic arrangement?
questions.explanation: The introductory material comes first, with the main subject and finite predicate delayed. This matches the lecture’s rhetorical description.
questions.example: After hours of waiting, the train at last appeared delays the principal statement.

options.text: The team’s arrival surprised us.
After several delays caused by heavy rain, the team finally arrived.
The team finally arrived, despite the rain and several delays.
The team arrived and unloaded its equipment.

questions.question: What is the main difference between the lecture’s loose and periodic versions of the arrival example?
questions.explanation: The versions can preserve the central event while organizing its presentation differently. Arrangement can change emphasis without changing every factual detail.
questions.example: The journey detail can precede or follow the arrival statement.

options.text: One version contains no grammatical structure
The tense must change from past to future
